Beyond Input Guardrails: Reconstructing Cross-Agent Semantic Flows for Execution-Aware Attack Detection

Yangyang Wei Affiliation: Department of Software Technology, Zhejiang University, Ningbo, China    Yijie Xu Affiliation: Department of Software Technology, Zhejiang University, Ningbo, China    Zhenyuan Li Affiliation: Department of Software Technology, Zhejiang University, Ningbo, China Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China Correspondence to: lizhenyuan@zju.edu.cn    Xiangmin Shen Affiliation: HOFSTRA University, Hangzhou, China    Shouling Ji Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract

Multi-Agent System is emerging as the de facto standard for complex task orchestration. However, its reliance on autonomous execution and unstructured inter-agent communication introduces severe risks, such as indirect prompt injection, that easily circumvent conventional input guardrails. To address this, we propose MAScope, a framework that shifts the defensive paradigm from static input filtering to execution-aware analysis. By extracting and reconstructing Cross-Agent Semantic Flows, MAScope synthesizes fragmented operational primitives into contiguous behavioral trajectories, enabling a holistic view of system activity. We leverage a Supervisor LLM to scrutinize these trajectories, identifying anomalies across data flow violations, control flow deviations, and intent inconsistencies. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that MAScope effectively detects over ten distinct compound attack vectors, achieving F1-scores of 85.3% and 66.7% for node-level and path-level end-to-end attack detection, respectively. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MAScope-71DC.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across expanding domains (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). However, when applied to complex, open-ended tasks, solitary models often face limited reasoning horizons and intrinsic hallucinations (Wei et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2023). To overcome these bottlenecks, Multi-Agent System (MAS) is emerging as the de facto standard for orchestrating intricate workflows, with platforms like AutoGen and LangGraph now managing millions of autonomous interactions daily across sectors ranging from automated software engineering to financial analysis. By integrating role specialization and collaborative planning, MAS can effectively address long-horizon reasoning challenges and decompose tasks that are otherwise intractable for single models (Li et al., 2024).

However, this architectural paradigm shift inherently expands the attack surface. By relying on autonomous execution and open-ended inter-agent communication, MAS introduces critical vulnerabilities, including indirect prompt injection and privilege escalation. Crucially, these systems do not merely expand the threat landscape quantitatively but complicate it qualitatively: vulnerabilities emerge not only from individual agent defects but also from the interaction dynamics, coordination logic, and transitive trust dependencies that permeate the system lifecycle (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025). These threats manifest across the entire execution spectrum, ranging from input-level prompt manipulation and interaction-stage memory poisoning or channel interception, to output-stage tool misuse, where dynamic delegation amplifies the cascading impact of unauthorized system modifications (Liu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), as Figure 1 shown.

A central challenge lies in the semantic ambiguity and execution fragmentation inherent to these threats. Unlike monolithic applications, MAS dissolves architectural boundaries, relying on agents driven by unstructured inputs and probabilistic logic. Consequently, attackers can orchestrate multi-step exploits by chaining seemingly innocuous micro-operations, fragmented across different agents and time steps, that only manifest as malicious when viewed as a complete sequence. Conventional input guardrails and sandboxing are rendered insufficient against such threats. They struggle to perform fine-grained extraction of critical fields from unstructured natural language interactions and lack the semantic situational awareness required to distinguish complex legitimate behaviors from malicious intent (Han et al., 2024). Thus, shifting from static input filtering to dynamic, execution-aware monitoring remains a formidable challenge.

To address this gap, this paper proposes MAScope, a unified framework that shifts the defensive paradigm to execution-aware analysis by observing and abstracting Cross-Agent Semantic Flows. Our methodology centers on three key innovations to tackle the aforementioned challenges. First, we address unstructured ambiguity by abstracting sensitive entities and operational primitives from raw interaction logs. Second, we tackle attack fragmentation by reconstructing contiguous behavioral execution trajectories from dispersed inter-agent communications and artifact manipulations. Finally, to resolve the benign-versus-malicious distinction, we leverage a dedicated Supervisor LLM to scrutinize these reconstructed flows, detecting anomalies across data flow violations, control flow deviations, and intent inconsistencies.

To evaluate the effectiveness of MAScope, we empirically reproduce the OWASP Top 10 attack techniques targeting various stages of the MAS lifecycle. By integrating these techniques into diverse operational scenarios, we synthesize and execute a series of compound attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that MAScope effectively abstracts sensitive fields, reconstructs suspicious behavioral trajectories, and successfully detects over ten distinct combinations of attack vectors. Quantitatively, the framework exhibits robust performance, attaining an F1-score of 76.8% for sensitive information extraction, along with F1-scores of 85.3% and 66.7% for node-level and path-level end-to-end attack detection, respectively.

All in all, our contributions can be concluded as follows:

  • •

    Methodology Proposal. We propose an innovative methodology that accurately identifies violations in data and control flows by abstracting sensitive entities from unstructured logs and reconstructing discrete communications into continuous behavioral trajectories.

  • •

    Semantic Flows Framework. We introduce the MAScope framework to transition the defense paradigm toward execution-aware analysis by analyzing cross-agent semantic flows.

  • •

    Empirical Evaluation. We reproduced the OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and complex attack scenarios for testing. The results demonstrate that MAScope accurately extracts sensitive fields, reconstructs suspicious trajectories, and successfully detects over ten types of combined attacks.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Emerging Multi-Agent System

While LLMs demonstrate remarkable versatility, their direct application to complex problem-solving is often constrained by intrinsic hallucinations and limited reasoning horizons. To address these limitations, MAS such as LangGraph11 1 LangGraph, https://www.langchain.com/langgraph, AutoGen22 2 AutoGen, https://microsoft.github.io/autogen, and MetaGPT33 3 MetaGPT, https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT have emerged, utilizing role-based orchestration and Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) to decompose intricate tasks into manageable sub-routines. Currently, these frameworks predominantly rely on sandboxed environments (e.g., Docker) and human-in-the-loop oversight to mitigate execution risks.

However, these measures often overlook the deeper architectural implications. Analogous to how microservices dismantled the boundaries of monolithic applications, thereby expanding the attack surface, MAS similarly dissolves the rigid constraints of deterministic software. That is, unlike traditional services bound by structured APIs, agents possess the autonomous capability to process unstructured data and maintain persistent context. Furthermore, MAS exhibits emergent collaborative intelligence through dynamic orchestration, intent alignment, and information sharing. This transition from rigid, formatted interactions to adaptive, general-purpose services, while enabling solutions for complex open environments, inherently introduces non-deterministic behavioral spaces and novel semantic security risks. To systematize these threats, the OWASP Foundation (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025) has categorized the Top 10 attack surfaces spanning the input, interaction, and output stages, as illustrated in Figure 1. Further details are provided in the Appendix A.

2.2 Defence for LLMs and LLM-based Agents

Guardrail-based defenses serve as the first line of defense, primarily mitigating threats such as prompt injection by intercepting, inspecting, and sanitizing model inputs and outputs (Dong et al., 2024; Inan et al., 2023). While effective in neutralizing single-turn adversarial exchanges, these approaches typically rely on static heuristics or context-agnostic filters. Consequently, they remain vulnerable to attacks that exploit multi-step reasoning, contextual dependencies, or semantic deception embedded across prolonged interaction histories.

To transcend the limitations of local I/O filtering, structural and graph-based approaches have emerged. These methods model agent interactions as graphs, identifying potential threats by analyzing propagation paths and applying structural interventions, such as edge pruning, to disrupt attack flows (Wang et al., 2025). However, their effectiveness is often predicated on the assumption that underlying models possess a baseline level of safety. Furthermore, they struggle to detect malicious intent when semantic manipulation is camouflaged within structurally valid interaction trajectories, effectively bypassing topology-based detection.

A parallel line of research focuses on pre-execution constraints and formal verification, aiming to synthesize deterministic safety policies that block unsafe actions prior to execution (Miculicich et al., 2025). While providing theoretical safety guarantees for isolated decision steps, these methods face significant scalability challenges in open-ended agentic environments. Crucially, they lack a holistic view of system-level state evolution, making it difficult to trace the causal origins of attacks or assess their impact on global system artifacts (e.g., file systems and network endpoints) across complex, multi-agent workflows.

3 Preliminaries

This section introduces the notation and formalizes the key concepts used throughout the paper. We define the structure of the Cross-Agent Semantic Graph and formulate two main problems in the threat detection task.

3.1 Cross-Agent Semantic Graph

Inspired by provenance-based threat detection (Li et al., 2021; Inam et al., 2023), we construct a semantic graph framework to characterize the cross-agent behavior of multi-agent systems. In a MAS, each interaction ee can be defined as a quintuple (l,s,r,o,t)(l,s,r,o,t), where ll, ss, rr, oo, and tt denote the layer, subject, relationship, object, and timestamp, respectively. Table 1 provides detailed mappings of the dependency relationships for different types of events. These events collectively form a MAS semantic graph GG, which is defined as:

G={e1,e2,…,en}\displaystyle G=\{e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}\} (1)

where each event ei=(li,si,ri,oi,ti)∈Ge_{i}=(l_{i},s_{i},r_{i},o_{i},t_{i})\in G denotes a temporal update to the graph structure.

3.2 Problem Definition

We formulate the detection of multi-stage attacks as a two-step optimization problem: mapping unstructured logs to structured semantic primitives, and then reconstructing causal flows to identify anomalies.

Semantic Primitives Extraction. Given a raw log entry u∈ℒu\in\mathcal{L} associated with a potential event, and a foundation model PθP_{\theta}, the goal is to extract a set of structured semantic primitives YY. These primitives include both Sensitive Entities (e.g., credentials, PII) and Operational Primitives (e.g., specific tool parameters).

We formulate this as a constraint-based conditional generation task. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the hierarchy of predefined sensitive categories. The extraction function f⁡(u,𝒞)f(u,\mathcal{C}) outputs a set of labeled pairs:

yi={(s,ℓ)∣(s,ℓ)∼Pθ​(Y∣u,τ𝒞)}y_{i}=\{(s,\ell)\mid(s,\ell)\sim P_{\theta}(Y\mid u,\tau_{\mathcal{C}})\} (2)

where ss is the extracted entity text, ℓ∈𝒞\ell\in\mathcal{C} is the semantic category, and τ𝒞\tau_{\mathcal{C}} represents the hierarchical constraint instructions (HSEC). The objective is to maximize the likelihood of correctly identifying all relevant entities yiy_{i} for every event eie_{i}, thereby populating the attributes of the semantic graph nodes.

Flow Reconstruction and Threat Detection. Locally, a single event eie_{i} may appear benign. To detect complex threats, we must analyze Behavioral Flows. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the space of all possible execution paths within graph GG. We define a candidate behavioral trajectory Tk∈ℋT_{k}\in\mathcal{H} as a time-ordered sequence of causally dependent events ending at a terminal node nn:

Tk=⟨ek1,ek2,…,ekm⟩,T_{k}=\langle e_{k_{1}},e_{k_{2}},\ldots,e_{k_{m}}\rangle, (3)

where ekj+1e_{k_{j+1}} depends on ekje_{k_{j}}.

The detection problem is to define a Flow Reconstruction Function Φ⁡(G)\Phi(G) that synthesizes fragmented events into candidate trajectories, and a Scrutiny Function 𝒮⁡(Tk)\mathcal{S}(T_{k}) (parameterized by the Supervisor LLM) that estimates the maliciousness of a trajectory. The goal is to identify the subset of optimal attack paths 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} that maximize the risk score:

𝒯∗={Tk∈Φ⁡(G)∣𝒮⁡(Tk)>δ}\mathcal{T}^{*}=\{T_{k}\in\Phi(G)\mid\mathcal{S}(T_{k})>\delta\} (4)

where 𝒮⁡(⋅)\mathcal{S}(\cdot) evaluates the trajectory against data flow, control flow, and intent consistency policies, and δ\delta is the decision threshold.

4 Method

As illustrated in Figure 2, MAScope comprises three interconnected modules: (1) a Data Collection Module that captures fine-grained interaction data between agents and system entities; (2) a Semantic Extracting & Flow Reconstruction Module that analyzes unstructured interaction logs to extract semantic primitives and synthesize execution flows; and (3) a Trajectory Scrutiny Module that audits these reconstructed paths to identify and detect latent attack vectors.

4.1 Data Collection in MAS

Building upon the formal definitions in §3, we operationalize the construction of the MAS semantic graph. It is crucial to recognize that while tool calls initiated by agents ultimately manifest as specific system events handled by kernel-level processes, relying exclusively on traditional kernel monitoring is insufficient to encompass the full observational scope of a MAS. Agents introduce high-level semantics, specifically intent, context, and reasoning chains, at the application layer, which typically elude capture by low-level kernel instrumentation.

To bridge this semantic gap and address the challenge of scattered, temporally inconsistent cross-layer data, we implement a dual-layer observation strategy. This involves integrating observations from both application and kernel layers, performing temporal alignment, and normalizing entity identifiers to uniformly incorporate heterogeneous data into the semantic graph. As illustrated in Figure 2, kernel collectors (e.g., ETW (, 2020), eBPF (, 2023)) are primarily responsible for monitoring the behavior of system process entities, while application-layer collectors (e.g., structured logging mechanisms (, 2026)) capture the high-level interactive behaviors of agents.

We denote each raw log record as a structured tuple containing rich contextual information:

Li={Logi,Subi,Obji}L_{i}=\{\text{Log}_{i},\text{Sub}_{i},\text{Obj}_{i}\} (5)

where Logi\text{Log}_{i} encompasses basic log attributes (e.g., timestamp, log type), Subi\text{Sub}_{i} denotes the subject context, and Obji\text{Obj}_{i} denotes the object context. Following acquisition, we deserialize and parse these records to instantiate the semantic event e=(l,s,r,o,t)e=(l,s,r,o,t) for subsequent graph construction and analysis.

4.2 Semantic Extracting & Flow Reconstruction

Following data collection, we parse unstructured interaction logs to identify sensitive information and reconstruct the multi-agent semantic graph. This phase entails two critical objectives: (i) the precise extraction of security-relevant entities from free-form context, and (ii) the quantitative assignment of sensitivity scores to prioritize suspicious paths for downstream scrutiny.

Directly applying general-purpose foundation models for open-domain sensitive information extraction often results in the retrieval of irrelevant entities and coarse-grained labels. This introduces significant noise, as the model may fail to distinguish benign references (e.g., city names in public news) from privacy-sensitive data (e.g., residential addresses), leading to both false positives and false negatives.

To mitigate these issues, we propose the Hierarchical Sensitive Entity Constraint (HSEC) mechanism. As illustrated in Figure 3, HSEC transforms abstract security knowledge into structured, hierarchical constraints. For instance, rather than a generic ”Location” label, HSEC maps entities to the subcategory Contact Information under the parent category Identity & Privacy. This hierarchical structure compels the model to evaluate entity attributes within an explicit risk context, significantly enhancing robustness against semantic ambiguity.

We formulate the extraction task as a constraint-based conditional sequence generation problem. Let xx denote the interaction content, encompassing agent messages, tool inputs/outputs, file paths, URLs, and associated kernel artifacts. Our goal is to predict a specific set of sensitive entities Y={y1,…,yn}Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\} and their corresponding sensitivity attributes via a mapping f⁡(x)→(Y,ℒ)f(x)\rightarrow(Y,\mathcal{L}). Specifically, HSEC constrains the model to generate triples (yi,ci,s​ci)(y_{i},c_{i},sc_{i}), where cic_{i} and s​cisc_{i} denote the top-level category and subcategory, respectively. Post-generation, we apply lightweight canonicalization ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) to normalize case, strip punctuation, and resolve relative file paths, ensuring graph consistency by storing ϕ⁡(yi)\phi(y_{i}).

Besides, we assign each extracted entity a continuous sensitivity score s⁡(y)∈[0,1]s(y)\in[0,1]. We decompose the score into a sensitive category prior and context adjustments:

s⁡(y)=b⁡(c,s​c)+Δctx​(y,x)s(y)=b(c,sc)+\Delta_{\text{ctx}}(y,x) (6)

Here, b⁡(c,s​c)b(c,sc) is a fixed base sensitivity weight per category and subcategory. For example, Credential & Secrets receives the highest base weight, Identity & Privacy is medium, and System & Infrastructure and Code & Payloads are medium-to-high depending on the subcategory. The context term Δctx\Delta_{\text{ctx}} captures security cues that cannot be represented by sensitive categories alone, computed deterministically from yy and its local context xx. Let πk​(y,x)∈{0,1}\pi_{k}(y,x)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether cue kk is present, where k∈{pat,ent,path,net}k\in\{\text{pat},\text{ent},\text{path},\text{net}\} correspond to (i) matching a secret-like pattern, (ii) high-entropy strings, (iii) sensitive file or directory paths, and (iv) appearing as an egress destination. The adjustment is computed as:

Δctx​(y)=∑kδk⋅𝕀⁡[πk​(y)],\Delta_{\text{ctx}}(y)=\sum_{k}\delta_{k}\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[\pi_{k}(y)\right], (7)

where δk\delta_{k} denotes the marginal risk contribution of cue kk.

To identify the most critical latent malicious behavioral trajectories for scrutiny, we prioritize candidate provenance paths based on aggregated risk. We define a weighted event risk score w⁡(ei)w(e_{i}) that integrates entity sensitivity, operation type, and target trustworthiness:

w(ei)=(∑y∈ℰ⁡(ei)s(y))⋅αri⋅(1+β⋅𝕀[d(oi)∉𝒯])w(e_{i})=\left(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{E}(e_{i})}s(y)\right)\cdot\alpha_{r_{i}}\cdot\left(1+\beta\cdot\mathbb{I}[d(o_{i})\notin\mathcal{T}]\right) (8)

where ℰ⁡(ei)\mathcal{E}(e_{i}) is the set of entities involved in event eie_{i}, and αri\alpha_{r_{i}} is a relation-dependent weight (assigning higher values to critical operations like IP_Send or File_Read). The term 𝕀[d(oi)∉𝒯]\mathbb{I}[d(o_{i})\notin\mathcal{T}] serves as a penalty factor, increasing the score by β\beta if the object’s domain d⁡(oi)d(o_{i}) does not belong to the trusted set 𝒯\mathcal{T} (e.g., known internal services).

Finally, we score a candidate provenance path H⁡(n)=⟨e1,…,em⟩H(n)=\langle e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\rangle ending at node nn by aggregating its constituent event scores with a temporal decay factor:

Score​(H⁡(n))=∑i=1mγ(tm−ti)⋅w⁡(ei)\text{Score}(H(n))=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\gamma^{(t_{m}-t_{i})}\cdot w(e_{i}) (9)

where γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] applies a mild recency discount to emphasize immediate threats while retaining historical context. The top-ranked paths are then forwarded to the Supervisor module for deep semantic verification.

4.3 Trajectory Scrutiny

To identify potential attacks in multi-agent systems, we design a supervisor module based on a foundation model that audits the reconstructed paths in the semantic graph against a set of rigorous security policies.

As illustrated in Figure 1, attacks on MAS typically manifest across the input, interaction, and output stages. A high-level analysis of complete attack causal chains reveals that successful exploits invariably distort one of three core dimensions: (1) the Data Flow (how information propagates between nodes); (2) the Control Flow (how authority and context are transferred); and (3) the Intent Alignment (whether the system’s actual behavior adheres to the user’s initial objective). Attacks achieve penetration by compromising these factors individually or in combination.

Based on this observation, we build three corresponding policies around these three types of factors to identify and intercept attack behaviors: intent consistency, data flow confidentiality, and control flow integrity, as shown in Table 2. In this table, H⁡(n)H(n) is a provenance path of time-ordered events associated with node nn, ssenss_{\text{sens}} is the set of sensitive entities, and oexto_{\text{ext}} is the set of untrusted external destinations on the path. sperms_{\text{perm}} and opermo_{\text{perm}} denote the privilege levels of the source and target nodes, respectively.

To evaluate intent consistency, we need an explicit representation of the user-approved intent for the current task. We obtain PintentP_{\text{intent}} from the initial user request and the agent’s declared plan. Concretely, we prompt a foundation model to produce a short structured intent specification that includes (i) the allowed goal(s), (ii) required resources (e.g., files, repositories, or tools) and their scopes, and (iii) explicit constraints (e.g., “do not exfiltrate data” or “do not contact external endpoints unless necessary”). We treat this structured intent specification as PintentP_{\text{intent}} and use it as the reference when checking whether a provenance path contains actions that deviate from the stated goal or violate stated constraints. In our implementation, PintentP_{\text{intent}} is generated once per session and can be optionally overridden by a user-defined policy template.

We define sensitive entities using a threshold on numeric sensitivity scores from §4.2:

ssens={y∣s⁡(y)≥τsens},s_{\text{sens}}=\{y\mid s(y)\geq\tau_{\text{sens}}\}, (10)

where τsens\tau_{\text{sens}} is a policy parameter. For confidentiality checks, we also identify untrusted external destinations on a path. For each event eie_{i} whose object oio_{i} is a network endpoint, we normalize the destination as:

d⁡(oi)={base_domain​(oi)if ​oi​ is a URL/domain,oiif ​oi​ is an IP address.d(o_{i})=\begin{cases}\text{base\_domain}(o_{i})&\text{if }o_{i}\text{ is a URL/domain},\\ o_{i}&\text{if }o_{i}\text{ is an IP address}.\end{cases} (11)

We mark oio_{i} as untrusted if d⁡(oi)∉𝒯d(o_{i})\notin\mathcal{T}, where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a configurable trusted set (e.g., allowlist domains, localhost, and private IP ranges), and define oext={d⁡(oi)∣d⁡(oi)∉𝒯}o_{\text{ext}}=\{d(o_{i})\mid d(o_{i})\notin\mathcal{T}\} for events on the path. The confidentiality policy then checks whether any sensitive entity flows to untrusted external destinations via ssens∩oext≠∅s_{\text{sens}}\cap o_{\text{ext}}\neq\emptyset.

We estimate the privilege level of each node using a foundation model conditioned on node attributes and local execution context. The input features include (i) process and user identity (e.g., user SID/UID, integrity level, token/role), (ii) execution context (e.g., parent process, service vs. interactive session), and (iii) operation type and object metadata (e.g., access to protected paths, registry hives, or privileged system calls). The model maps these signals to an ordinal privilege level (e.g., low, user, admin/root). We assign sperms_{\text{perm}} and opermo_{\text{perm}} to the source and target nodes by applying this estimator to their associated context on the provenance path.

Given PintentP_{\text{intent}} and the selected provenance path H⁡(n)H(n), the supervisor evaluates whether any policy is violated (intent consistency, confidentiality, or integrity). The supervisor outputs (i) a binary decision y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} indicating whether a violation is detected, and (ii) a short evidence string that cites concrete event attributes (e.g., destination d⁡(o)d(o), tool names, file paths, or commands) to make alerts explainable.

5 Experiment

In this section, we conduct experimental evaluations to answer two research questions, namely, RQ1. To what extent can MAScope accurately extract sensitive entities and operational primitives from unstructured agent interactions? and RQ2. How effective is MAScope in reconstructing multi-stage behavioral trajectories and detecting compound attack vectors against benign baselines?

5.1 Experiment Setup

Dataset. To evaluate the efficacy of MAScope, we construct 10 high-fidelity simulation scenarios utilizing the LangGraph framework. These scenarios encapsulate a diverse range of real-world applications, including: (S1) Corporate Recruitment Platforms, (S2) Automated Email Orchestration Systems, (S3) Collaborative Programming Copilots, (S4) Conversational Knowledge Assistants, and (S5) Enterprise Database Infrastructures. Adversarial models are aligned with the OWASP Top 10 attack surface for LLM Applications as detailed in Appendix C. Unlike static evaluations, each testbed involves complex multi-turn agentic interactions, with logs collected via application-layer telemetry and system-level audit logs. This process yields a dataset of 14,927 records. To establish ground truth, we performed fine-grained log analysis to manually label three distinct categories: (1) sensitive entities for extraction tasks, (2) critical attack paths for reconstruction efficacy, and (3) malicious nodes for final threat detection.

Model. We employed state-of-the-art LLMs to evaluate the performance of MAScope. Specifically, we utilized ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 for the sensitive entity extraction task. For the path reconstruction and policy analysis phases, we leveraged ChatGPT-5.2 to identify entities and interpret detection rules, capitalizing on its advanced reasoning capabilities. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, ChatGPT-5.2 also serves as the primary backbone for our proposed Supervisor agent. The comprehensive system prompts and operational instructions for which are detailed in Appendix B.

Baseline. We establish a VanillaGPT baseline using a standalone instance of ChatGPT-5.2. To ensure a fair comparison, this baseline was prompted with the exact same set of security detection rules as MAScope but lacked our semantic flow reconstruction framework. This setup restricts the baseline to identifying potential alerts directly from raw execution logs, allowing us to quantify the specific performance gains attributable to our cross-agent semantic reconstruction capabilities.

Experimental Setting. The proposed framework is implemented in Python 3.10 to utilize its native support for dataclasses and asynchronous orchestration. The core anomaly detection and tag propagation logic rely on standard libraries like asyncio and json to ensure deterministic provenance graph processing. For semantic analysis, the OpenAI-compatible client is used to invoke ChatGPT for entity extraction and policy evaluation. Experiments are conducted on a Windows 11 system powered by an AMD Ryzen 7 5800H processor and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 GPU.

5.2 Effectiveness of Semantic Extracting

We systematically evaluate the effectiveness of Hierarchical Sensitive Entity Constraint Hints (HSEC) on the OWASP Top-10 dataset. As shown in Table 3, HSEC achieves significant improvements across both backbone models. For Gemini-3, the overall F1 score improves from 48.2% to 75.7%, an increase of 27.5%. Precision and recall rise to 73.6% and 77.9%, respectively. Similarly, for GPT-5.2, the overall F1 score improves from 49.4% to 76.8%, an increase of 27.4%. Precision and recall also increase to 75.7% and 77.9%, respectively. These results demonstrate that HSEC is highly effective in enhancing sensitive entity extraction.

HSEC consistently improves extraction performance across various attack types, particularly in categories where baseline models perform poorly. For example, Gemini-3 achieves significant improvements in categories ①, ③, ⑧, and ⑩, with F1 scores rising substantially from a low baseline to a competitive level. This is because when the sensitive entity involves source code, baseline models tend to identify only fragmented snippets, whereas HSEC recognizes the code as a semantically complete logical block. We attribute these improvements to the unique strengths of HSEC in sensitive information extraction. HSEC places entity identification within hierarchical constraints and explicit risk contexts, guiding the model to operate within defined security boundaries. This mechanism effectively mitigates semantic ambiguity and cross-category confusion, thereby reducing the misclassification of generic entities as risky ones.

5.3 Effectiveness of Attack Detection

We systematically evaluate the threat detection capabilities of MAScope, with Table 4 presenting a comprehensive comparative analysis against the Vanilla GPT baseline. Our evaluation begins with an assessment of path-level detection efficacy. To ensure a rigorous and unbiased comparison, we normalize the evaluation granularity to the node level. This approach enables a high-fidelity assessment of alert accuracy across all critical nodes within the execution path.

As summarized in Table 4, the path-based detection component of MAScope attains a precision of 81.3% and an F1-score of 66.7%. Furthermore, the overall threat detection results demonstrate a clear performance advantage of MAScope. It achieves an overall precision of 96.5%, a recall of 76.4%, and an F1-score of 85.3%. By contrast, the Vanilla GPT baseline performs poorly, with a precision of only 23.1%, a recall of 20.8%, and an F1-score of 21.9%, which are substantially lower than those of MAScope.

The superior performance of MAScope is primarily attributed to its capability to reconstruct fragmented system events into coherent behavioral trajectories. For instance, in our first case study, when two distinct attack paths converge at a common node, MAScope intelligently consolidates them into a unified trajectory to maintain structural integrity. While this conservative approach may marginally impact the system’s recall, it effectively filters out background noise and ensures the high-fidelity detection of critical attack chains. In contrast to Vanilla GPT, which relies on context-agnostic reasoning and fails to capture multi-step semantic dependencies, MAScope leverages semantic flow tracking to precisely distinguish latent malicious intent from complex but legitimate agent operations.

5.4 Case Study

As shown in Figure 4, an external attacker leveraged a multi-agent system to steal personally identifiable information and spread malicious emails. To carry out this attack, the attacker sent an email containing a prompt injection to the system. The Email Agent processed this input through the Gmail process and forwarded the malicious context to the Planning Agent. Under the control of the injected instructions, the Planning Agent invoked the Data Agent, which executed an SQL query to read the Staff Database and extract sensitive employee email addresses. Finally, the Planning Agent invoked the Internal Agent to utilize this stolen information. The Internal Agent used the Gmail tool to send outgoing emails to the victim employees, thus completing the data theft.

In this attack scenario, MAScope successfully reconstructs the complete attack lifecycle. Upon detecting the internal agent sending emails to internal employees, MAScope automatically traces and inspects the execution path originating from the data agent. As illustrated in Figure 4, this path involves extensive interactions with sensitive entities and is consequently flagged as a data leakage anomaly. This detection accurately captures the full chain of malicious behavior. In contrast, VanillaGPT underperforms in this scenario due to its tendency to evaluate actions in isolation. It misclassifies the internal agent’s use of Gmail for internal communication as normal traffic and the data agent’s query for employee records as routine behavior, failing to recognize the malicious intent concealed within this sequence of coordinated actions.

6 Conclusion

This paper addresses the critical security voids in MAS, where autonomous execution renders traditional input guardrails insufficient. We proposed MAScope, a novel framework that shifts the defensive paradigm to execution-aware analysis by reconstructing cross-agent semantic flows. By bridging the semantic gap between high-level agent intents and low-level kernel artifacts, our methodology effectively isolates fragmented, multi-stage threats that evade static detection. Empirical evaluations against the OWASP Top 10 attacks demonstrate that MAScope robustly detects complex, compound attack vectors, validating the superiority of dynamic trajectory scrutiny over static filtering. These findings establish a foundational pathway for securing future agentic ecosystems against emergent, compositional risks.

Impact Statement

This work addresses the critical security gap impeding the safe adoption of MAS. By elevating threat detection from static, rule-based monitoring to semantic behavioral analysis, MAScope enables the identification of sophisticated, multi-step attacks that bypass conventional sandboxing. This paradigm shift establishes a foundation for trustworthy agentic computing, ensuring that the autonomous capabilities of MAS can be deployed in complex, open-ended environments without compromising data confidentiality or system integrity.

Appendix A Expanded Attack Surface in Multi-Agent Systems

Compared to single-agent systems, MAS substantially expand and complicate the attack surface, with security risks arising not only from individual agent vulnerabilities but also from the interactions, coordination, and dependencies among agents. Such attacks may span the entire lifecycle of agentic systems (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025). Figure 1 illustrates various attack paths.

At the input stage, agents struggle to reliably distinguish valid instructions from contextual data due to the inherent semantic ambiguity of natural language. Adversaries can exploit this via Indirect Prompt Injection, leveraging falsified tool outputs or contaminated external data to redirect agent goals, planning, and multi-step behaviors (Lee and Tiwari, 2024). Furthermore, structural mismatches between user-centric identity models and agent architectures facilitate privilege escalation through dynamic delegation and trust inheritance mechanisms (Huang et al., 2025). Additionally, anthropomorphic agent behaviors may be leveraged to induce excessive user trust, widening the social engineering surface (Herdel et al., 2024).

During the interaction stage, reliance on persistent memory and extended context introduces risks of Memory Poisoning, where injected malicious data biases reasoning and triggers unsafe tool usage (Chen et al., 2024). Decentralized inter-agent communication, often characterized by asymmetric trust, undermines traditional boundary defenses, making interception and session manipulation critical vectors (He et al., 2025). Crucially, compromised agents may exhibit emergent malignancy—behaviors that appear benign locally but precipitate destructive system-level outcomes through cascading interactions (Kulshreshtha et al., 2025).

At the output stage, risks manifest primarily through Tool Misuse, where misaligned objectives or ambiguous instructions lead to the improper execution of legitimate capabilities (Lee and Tiwari, 2024). Across the broader lifecycle, the dynamic runtime composition of third-party models and tools transforms the agentic supply chain into a live attack surface (Boisvert et al., 2025). Moreover, agents’ ability to generate and execute code can be exploited to escape sandboxed environments or trigger remote code execution (Guo et al., 2024), while localized failures may be amplified through autonomous planning and persistent states, ultimately compromising system confidentiality, integrity, and availability (Cemri et al., 2025).

Appendix B Prompt Construction

This section details the prompt engineering architectures for sensitive information extraction, policy compliance auditing, VanillaGPT baseline configurations, and adversarial designs for six distinct attacks.

Appendix C OWASP Top 10 Attacks

This section summarizes the major attack types in the OWASP Agentic AI Top 10 that are most relevant to agentic systems.

Agent Goal Hijack The attacker hosts a spoofed website embedding a malicious prompt. When the agent ingests the page during task execution, the prompt hijacks the agent’s goal, overrides the user’s objectives and constraints, and induces unauthorized actions, including extracting sensitive database records and exfiltrating them via email.

Tool Misuse and Exploitation The attacker emails a malicious prompt to the victim. When the agent ingests it during inbox summarization, the prompt exploits tool access, causing the agent to misuse its contacts and email-sending tools to harvest the address book and automatically send phishing messages, thereby propagating through the victim’s social graph.

Identity and Privilege Abuse The attacker inserts a high-privilege intermediary agent into the review-and-forward path and abuses its identity and permissions to rewrite the user’s legitimate request into a malicious task. The downstream executor then uses the inherited privileges to access the database and exfiltrate sensitive records via email.

Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities The attacker compromises the agent supply chain by planting a malicious prompt in a file agent’s tool description. When the planner ingests this untrusted metadata, it generates an unauthorized plan that reads sensitive database records and exfiltrates them via email.

Unexpected Code Execution A spoofed website embeds a malicious prompt that contaminates a coding agent’s context and causes it to generate code with hidden malicious logic. When the user runs this output, it triggers unexpected code execution that reads sensitive local files (e.g., credentials/keys) and exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

Memory and Context Poisoning Through memory and context poisoning, the attacker contaminates the RAG instruction library, so retrieved guidance injects covert malicious logic into generated code. When executed, the code reads sensitive data and exfiltrates it to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

Insecure Inter Agent Communication By exploiting insecure inter-agent communication, the attacker tampers with the file agent’s output and injects malicious directives that downstream agents execute as trusted state, triggering unauthorized database reads and email exfiltration to the attacker.

Cascading Failures A resume-borne prompt hijacks the agent’s goal and is forwarded as trusted intermediate output, causing cascading failures across downstream agents that culminate in unauthorized database access and email exfiltration to the attacker.

Human Agent Trust Exploitation The attacker plants a malicious prompt in a resume that exploits human trust in the workflow, convincing the user that a password is required to proceed and to email it to an attacker-controlled address, resulting in credential theft.

Rogue Agents A rogue agent injects a malicious prompt into its response, which downstream agents trust and execute as guidance. This propagates through the workflow and triggers unauthorized tool use, including reading the backend database and exfiltrating the contents via email to the attacker.

C.1 Case Study

Case 3. In this attack, the attackers introduced an untrusted fake agent into the multi-agent system with the aim of stealing internal database information and leaking it. To carry out the attack, the attackers first manipulated the fake agent to establish a connection and interact with the system’s core component, the Planning Agent, injecting a malicious command context. As a result, the Planning Agent mistakenly trusted the command and subsequently invoked the Data Agent. The Data Agent executed an SQL query, illegally reading the Staff Database containing sensitive employee information. Subsequently, the Planning Agent invoked the Email Agent, using the Gmail process to send the stolen sensitive data to an external network address controlled by the attackers, completing the illegal data leakage.

In this scenario, MAScope first extracts sensitive information from the unstructured data of each interaction and generates a semantic graph using cross-source data collection. As shown in Figure 7, when the Email Agent is detected sending data packets containing sensitive information to an unknown external network, MAScope traces the entire call chain, focusing on the complete path from the fake agent’s intervention to the final data leakage. Finally, it triggers alerts for user intent inconsistency and sensitive information leakage.

Case 5. In this attack, external attackers used a malicious webpage to inject indirect hints, inducing a multi-agent system to execute remote code and steal sensitive credentials. To carry out the attack, the attackers first tricked the Web Agent into visiting a malicious webpage containing hidden malicious instructions. The Web Agent ingested the malicious instructions while processing the webpage content and passed them as context to the Planning Agent. As a result, the Planning Agent instructed the Code Agent to write a script file named sqldump.sh (potentially for masquerading or subsequent exploitation), which then invoked the Executor Agent to execute shell commands. Driven by the malicious instructions, the Executor Agent used a bash process to read the system’s highly sensitive SSH private key file and sent this credential directly to an external IP address controlled by the attacker, completing the high-risk credential theft.

In Figure 14, when the code generated by sqldump.sh was detected, MAScope detected an inconsistency with the user’s intent and generated an alert. When MAScope detects that the Executor Agent calls the Bash process to establish a connection with the external network, it will focus on examining the data flow path from the Agent to the external IP, because this path involves the sensitive file entity .ssh/rsa. In Figure 4, this path is identified as an anomaly of sensitive credential leakage because it clearly shows the malicious behavior pattern of the Agent, after generating a suspicious script, illegally reading core cryptographic credentials and sending them to untrusted external nodes.

Case 9. In this attack, an external attacker implemented indirect password injection by tampering with a job application file, aiming to steal user passwords using a system agent. The attacker first embedded hidden malicious instructions in the resume file. When the File Agent read the file content through a shell process and relayed it to the Planning Agent, the malicious context was activated. Simultaneously, the user provided sensitive password information to the Planning Agent. Misled by the injected instructions, the Planning Agent passed the context containing the password to the Assistant Agent. Subsequently, the Assistant Agent improperly invoked the shell process, directly sending the intercepted password to an external network address controlled by the attacker.

In this scenario, MAScope first extracted sensitive information from the unstructured data of each interaction and generated a semantic graph using cross-source data collection. In the analysis of this scenario, MAScope focused on monitoring the calls from the Planning Agent to the Assistant Agent and then to the shell. This path was identified as a control flow anomaly because the system detected that the Assistant Agent deviated from predefined behavioral norms, unexpectedly and improperly invoking the underlying shell process for external network communication. This unexpected agent invocation behavior disrupted the system’s established control flow integrity, thus triggering an alert.

Case 10. In this attack, an external attacker used a maliciously crafted prompt file to inject malicious information into a multi-agent system, aiming to steal sensitive internal data. To carry out the attack, the attacker first submitted a prompt file containing malicious instructions. The File Agent invoked the go process to process the file and passed the parsed malicious context to the core Planning Agent. Controlled by the injected instructions, the Planning Agent directed the Data Agent to execute an SQL query, illegally reading sensitive employee information (PII: staff info) from the Staff Database. Subsequently, the Planning Agent further invoked the Email Agent, using the Gmail process to directly send the acquired sensitive data to an external IP address controlled by the attacker, completing the illegal data leakage.

In this scenario, MAScope first extracted sensitive information from the unstructured data of each interaction and generated a semantic graph using cross-source data collection. In Figure 10, when the Email Agent was detected sending data to an unknown external network, MAScope traced back the data flow, focusing on examining the complete path from the Data Agent obtaining data to the Email Agent sending data. In Figure 16, this path was identified as an anomaly in the leakage of sensitive information because it fully records the unauthorized process of sensitive data (employee information) being extracted from a protected database and flowing to an untrusted external node via an email channel.
